facts.value: Alibaba and Tencent (strategic equity investors / Chinese cloud providers)
facts.excerpt: Alibaba Group Holding and Tencent Holdings are among a band of prominent Chinese Big Tech companies and venture capital (VC) firms that have helped start-up Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co (Zhipu
facts.notes: This is an EQUITY INVESTMENT relationship (Alibaba, Tencent, Ant Group, Meituan, Xiaomi, HongShan, GL Ventures et al.), NOT a disclosed compute-supply or cloud-lease contract. The article names no cloud/compute infrastructure terms. Included because Alibaba Cloud/Tencent Cloud are the lab's known partners; no rented MW capacity is attributable to Zhipu from this. Amount US$342M is total 2023 fundraising, not infrastructure capex.

verification.verifier_note: SCMP (Oct 20, 2023) states 'Alibaba Group Holding and Tencent Holdings are among a band of prominent Chinese Big Tech companies... [that] helped start-up... Zhipu AI raise a total of 2.5 billion yuan (US$342 million)' and both took part in the Series B3 round. Matches value, site, and date.

facts.value: Huawei (Z.ai/GLM models adapted to run on Huawei Ascend and Kirin chips; cloud-device collaboration)
facts.excerpt: The tie-up marks a major breakthrough in cloud-device collaboration between home-grown large [language] models and computational architecture, highlighting the deeper integration of a domestic AI ecos
facts.notes: Hardware/ecosystem partnership with Huawei (Ascend server chips + Kirin device chips), not Zhipu-owned capacity. No MW, chip count, or datacenter site given. English secondary reporting; translation/secondary-source uncertainty.

verification.verifier_note: SCMP (Aug 9, 2025) states GLM models are 'now compatible with Huawei's Ascend processors... and Kirin chips' and describes 'a major breakthrough in cloud-device collaboration.' Matches value, site, and date.

facts.value: Huawei Ascend Atlas 800T A2 (used to train Zhipu's GLM-Image model)
facts.excerpt: Huawei's Ascend Atlas 800T A2 server, incorporating the company's in-house Ascend AI processors ... MindSpore, Huawei's all-in-one machine learning framework
facts.notes: Compute HARDWARE attributed to Huawei, NOT a Zhipu-owned facility. Zhipu (US Entity List since Jan 2025) trains on Huawei Ascend instead of Nvidia. No chip count, cluster location, power (MW), or datacenter site disclosed. English secondary reporting on a Chinese-language disclosure; translation/secondary-source uncertainty.

verification.verifier_note: SCMP (Jan 14, 2026) literally states 'the entire training pipeline for GLM-Image, from data preparation to the final training run, was conducted on Huawei's Ascend Atlas 800T A2 server' using Huawei Ascend processors and MindSpore. Value, site (huawei-ascend), and date all match.

facts.value: Huawei (GLM-5 deep inference adaptation on Chinese-made chip clusters)
facts.excerpt: Zhipu AI's new GLM-5 large language model has completed deep inference adaptation with Huawei, ensuring the model's stable operation on Chinese-made chip clusters.
facts.notes: Describes inference deployment on domestic chip clusters (also adapted to Moore Threads, Cambricon), NOT a Zhipu-owned cluster. Widely reported in secondary/tech-blog sources that GLM-5 was TRAINED on ~100,000 Huawei Ascend 910B chips, but that figure is not confirmed by Zhipu and I could not verify it verbatim on a primary/reputable page, so it is NOT recorded as a gpu_count. Chinese-lab disclosure; secondary-source uncertainty.

verification.verifier_note: Caixin (Feb 12, 2026) states 'GLM-5 large language model has completed deep inference adaptation with Huawei, ensuring the model's stable operation on Chinese-made chip clusters.' Matches value, site, and date exactly.

facts.excerpt: in early talks with domestic chip-design companies about tailored AI processors
facts.notes: EXPLORATORY ONLY, not a committed program. Per The Information (via SCMP and TrendForce 2026-07-08), Zhipu is in preliminary/early talks with domestic chip-design houses about a custom ASIC for the GLM family; no partner selected (Cambricon and Biren cited only as candidate designers), and a viable ASIC is estimated at >2 years out. Motivated by GLM-5.2 usage surging ~27x and Nvidia export restrictions. Secondary sourcing (SCMP/TrendForce citing The Information); no in-house tapeout, foundry, or chip announced.

verification.verifier_note: SCMP (Jul 9, 2026) reports Zhipu was only 'in early talks with domestic chip-design companies about tailored AI processors' per The Information. This is exploratory/preliminary talks, NOT an 'announced' custom-silicon program. Status mismatch: fact claims status='announced' but the page supports at

facts.excerpt: Z.ai, the developer of the GLM family of AI models, has completed construction of a 1GW-class AI data center using only Chinese-made AI chips, with part of the facility already operating.
facts.notes: FIRST owned-capacity fact for Zhipu; ledger previously held only cloud_partnership/custom_silicon. Source states '1GW-class' / '1-gigawatt'; recorded as 1,000 MW per MW-only rule (no other arithmetic). IMPORTANT CAVEAT for the verifier: construction is complete but only PART of the facility is operating as of 2026-07-21, so 'operational' should not be read as 1,000 MW fully energised; no source gives an MW figure for the live portion. Ultimate reporting is Bloomberg (2026-07-20) citing a person familiar with the matter; TechNode credits Bloomberg. SCMP (2026-07-21) independently reports 'it had built a giant 1-gigawatt (GW) AI computing centre' per people familiar. Location, cost and construction timeline are NOT disclosed by any source (Tom's Hardware: 'The source didn't disclose the data center's location, its cost, or its construction timeline.'). Site slug is descriptive, not a place name.

verification.verifier_note: TechNode says '1GW-class' with 'part of the facility already operating' and gives no MW figure for the live portion; 1,000 MW at status operational is unsupported (class/design capacity, partial energisation).

facts.excerpt: it had built a giant 1-gigawatt (GW) AI computing centre – a facility that will be used to train and deploy its GLM models
facts.notes: Ownership basis: SCMP and TechNode both attribute the build to Z.ai itself ('has completed construction', 'it had built'), i.e. self-built rather than rented cloud capacity, which is why this is owned_facility rather than cloud_partnership per DECISIONS.md §1. Caveat: no source states a legal ownership/lease structure, a site operator, or a landlord; the claim rests on 'people familiar with the matter' (SCMP) / a person familiar (Bloomberg via TechNode and Tom's Hardware). Same SCMP piece reports Z.ai completed the acquisition of Chinese heterogeneous-computing software developer XCore Sigma (中科加禾), spun off from the Chinese Academy of Sciences — a vertical-integration move with no matching metric in the schema enum, recorded here for context only.

verification.verifier_note: Excerpt verbatim; SCMP attributes the build to Z.ai itself ('the company recently completed', 'it had built'), per people familiar. Caveat: use of the site is future tense ('will be used').

facts.value: 1GW-class AI computing centre built by Z.ai and populated exclusively with Chinese-made AI chips, to train and deploy the GLM model family; location undisclosed
facts.excerpt: Chinese AI developer Z.ai (formerly Zhipu) has finished building a 1GW data center stocked exclusively with domestically made chips and has switched part of it on, Bloomberg reported Monday
facts.notes: Site-record companion to the power_capacity_mw fact. Only part of the site is switched on as of 2026-07-21. Chip vendor is NOT named by the source: 'The source didn't name the chip supplier, but Z.ai's recent training history points to Huawei.' Tom's Hardware is relaying Bloomberg's 2026-07-20 report; treat as secondary. Same article notes the site is 'among the largest built by any Chinese model developer'.

verification.verifier_note: Excerpt verbatim; page supports built by Z.ai, exclusively domestic chips, part switched on, location/cost/timeline undisclosed, but says the facility 'will train' the GLM family, not 'deploy'.

facts.excerpt: the source told Bloomberg that Z.ai has now built or operates several computing clusters holding more than 10,000 chips apiece
facts.notes: Conservative low end: source says 'more than 10,000 chips apiece' across 'several' clusters, so 10,000 is the floor for a SINGLE cluster, not the fleet total; no total is stated and none is computed here. Chips are Chinese-made accelerators, vendor unnamed. 'built or operates' leaves owned-vs-rented ambiguous — do NOT read this as a confirmed owned fleet. Attribution: Bloomberg (2026-07-20) via Tom's Hardware; TechNode carries the same Bloomberg line ('Z.ai also operates several computing clusters containing more than 10,000 chips each').

verification.verifier_note: Excerpt verbatim: 'several computing clusters holding more than 10,000 chips apiece' — 10,000 is a floor for ONE cluster, not a fleet total, as the notes state. 'built or operates' leaves owned-vs-rented open.

facts.excerpt: it says the GLM-5 family was trained on roughly 100,000 Huawei Ascend 910B processors using the MindSpore framework, with no Nvidia silicon at any stage
facts.notes: Company self-claim relayed by Tom's Hardware ('it says' = Z.ai), NOT independently confirmed and NOT an Epoch AI / SemiAnalysis estimate. The 100,000 Ascend 910B figure is the chip count used to TRAIN the GLM-5 family; the source does not say whether Z.ai owns these accelerators or accessed them via a partner/cloud, so this must not be treated as a confirmed owned fleet — site slug reuses the existing 'huawei-ascend' slug already in the ledger. Source word is 'roughly'; recorded as stated with no rounding of our own. Same article: Z.ai on the US Entity List since January 2025, cutting off Nvidia H100/H200/B200.

verification.verifier_note: Page frames it as Z.ai's own claim ('it says', 'purportedly'): GLM-5 family trained on 'roughly' 100,000 Ascend 910B. No statement Z.ai owns or operates them; a training-run count, not an operational fleet.

facts.value: Prospectus disclosure: by 2025 all five of Zhipu's largest suppliers were cloud computing providers, and every cloud supplier on its disclosed list is Chinese
facts.excerpt: By 2025, however, all of its top-five suppliers were cloud computing providers.
facts.notes: Read of Zhipu's HKEX IPO prospectus by ChinaTalk (Irene Zhang); figures are the analyst's rendering of the prospectus, not a first-party Zhipu statement, and the prospectus itself was not fetched. Establishes that as of 2025 Zhipu's compute was predominantly RENTED from Chinese cloud providers → cloud_partnership, not owned capacity, per DECISIONS.md §1. Same piece: 'In 2022 and 2023, some of the company's largest purchases were sourced from suppliers of "computing hardware" rather than "computer services" ... implying some degree of local compute.' Individual supplier names are anonymised in the prospectus. Zhipu listed on HKEX 2026-01-08.

verification.verifier_note: Excerpt verbatim; page also states 'All of the cloud suppliers on Zhipu's disclosed list are Chinese.' Analyst read of the HKEX prospectus, as the notes already flag.

facts.value: Public open call to domestic and international inference-compute providers to supply capacity for GLM models in exchange for revenue share
facts.excerpt: Zhipu last week issued appeals to both domestic and international inference-compute providers to offer support for its GLM model, offering to share revenue.
facts.notes: Evidence of a serving-capacity shortfall five months before the 1GW site was reported complete: SCMP says it was 'the first time a Chinese AI firm issued a public call seeking computing resources' and that shares fell ~23% (>HK$70 billion / US$9 billion of market cap) on computing-constraint concerns. Status 'announced' because it is a solicitation — no counterparty, capacity or contract is named in the source. Useful trend context alongside SCMP 3341000 (2026-01), which reported computing constraints forcing Zhipu to restrict sign-ups for its AI coding service.

verification.verifier_note: Excerpt verbatim on SCMP 2026-02-23; page adds it was 'the first time a Chinese AI firm issued a public call seeking computing resources'. No counterparty or capacity named, consistent with 'announced'.
